orders.reason: months of intermittent abdominal pain with bloody diarrhea

documents.title: Primary Care Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: blood in stool, abdominal cramping

HPI: Since around the start of the summer she has had intermittent crampy lower abdominal pain with loose stools and blood mixed in. Some days fine, other days up to 6 BMs, with urgency and a feeling she hasn't finished. Did not mention it in June because "it came and went" and she thought it was hemorrhoids. No fever, no travel, no new foods, no antibiotics this year. No NSAIDs. Appetite ok.
Colonoscopy 2018 normal, father had colon cancer.

Exam: VS as charted, afebrile. Appears comfortable, a little anxious. Abd soft, mild tenderness in lower abdomen diffusely, no rebound or guarding, no masses. Rectal deferred to GI given planned scope.

A/P: Chronic intermittent hematochezia and diarrhea x ~5 months, 67 y/o, FH colon cancer, on MTX/prednisone. Ddx inflammatory colitis vs neoplasm vs infection less likely given duration.
- Stool C. diff and stool culture today.
- GI referral for colonoscopy - asked for first available; she was due for her 5-year scope in 2023 anyway.
- Return precautions: heavy bleeding, fever, lightheadedness, severe pain -> call same day.

documents.title: Stool tests
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Arlene - your stool tests show no infection (C. difficile and the culture were both negative). That makes the colonoscopy all the more important. GI's office has the referral; their scheduler should call you this week. If you don't hear by Monday, let us know and we'll push.

documents.title: RE: Stool tests
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Thank you. They called already, I'm scheduled for the 26th of December. Not how I wanted to spend the holiday week but I'd rather get it done.

reports.text: Specimens: colon biopsies, multiple sites from rectum proximally. Microscopic: colonic mucosa with active chronic colitis, crypt abscesses, crypt distortion and surface ulceration. No granulomas. No dysplasia identified. No viral cytopathic effect.
reports.conclusion: Active chronic colitis with crypt abscesses and mucosal ulceration, consistent with ulcerative colitis in the appropriate clinical and endoscopic setting. Negative for dysplasia.

documents.title: Gastroenterology consultation and colonoscopy
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
GASTROENTEROLOGY
Patient: Arlene Jacobs   DOB 01/30/1955
Date of service: 12/26/2022
Referring: primary care

History: 67-year-old woman with about six months of intermittent abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. On bad days she has as many as six bowel movements, with urgency and incomplete evacuation. Stool infectious studies from your office were negative. Past history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate and prednisone 5 mg, osteoporosis on alendronate, and breast cancer treated in 2016. No allergies. Former smoker, light alcohol. Father had colon cancer.

Exam: mildly uncomfortable. Abdomen with mild diffuse tenderness, no rebound or guarding. Rectal: no masses; bright red blood on the examining glove.

Labs (12/26): hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, WBC 9,000, platelets 310,000, CRP 24 mg/L, ESR 40 mm/hr.

Colonoscopy (12/26): continuous inflammation beginning at the rectum and extending proximally, with erythema, loss of the normal vascular pattern and multiple superficial ulcers. Biopsies taken. No masses or polyps seen.

Pathology (12/30): active chronic colitis with crypt abscesses and mucosal ulceration, no dysplasia.

Impression: new diagnosis of ulcerative colitis. Hemoglobin 11.2, likely from blood loss and inflammation.

Plan:
1. Mesalamine 800 mg tablets, one three times daily. Prescription sent.
2. She stays on prednisone 5 mg for her RA; no additional steroid for now.
3. GI follow-up in about 3 months, sooner for worsening bleeding.
4. Recheck CBC with her next methotrexate labs.

Gastroenterology

documents.title: Colitis medicine
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Dr., the GI doctor told me I have ulcerative colitis and started me on mesalamine three times a day. Two weeks in and the bleeding is less already. Do I need to tell my rheumatologist? And can your office refill the mesalamine or does it have to be GI? Arlene

documents.title: RE: Colitis medicine
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Good to hear it's already helping. I've added ulcerative colitis and mesalamine to your chart, and I'll send the GI note to rheumatology so they're aware. GI should handle mesalamine refills for now while they're adjusting things; we can take over later if that's easier. Your next methotrexate labs in early March will include a blood count to make sure the anemia is improving.

documents.title: Endocrinology follow-up
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
ENDOCRINOLOGY FOLLOW-UP
Arlene Jacobs   DOB 01/30/1955   Seen 03/13/2023

Ms. Jacobs returns for postmenopausal osteoporosis, diagnosed two years ago and treated with alendronate since then. Since I last saw her she was diagnosed with ulcerative colitis by GI and started mesalamine. She also has a history of breast cancer, treated in 2016. She takes her medicines reliably and has no new complaints. No falls and no fractures.

Medications include alendronate 70 mg weekly, calcium carbonate/vitamin D3 twice daily, prednisone 5 mg daily, methotrexate, mesalamine, HCTZ, amlodipine and atorvastatin. Former smoker; social alcohol. Family history notable for her mother's hip fracture at 72.

Exam: height is 2 cm less than two years ago (160 cm); weight stable. Otherwise unremarkable.

Labs 03/06: calcium 9.8, phosphorus 3.5, alkaline phosphatase 70, TSH 2.1, 25-OH vitamin D 32.
DXA 03/08: lumbar spine T-score -2.5, improved from -3.0 at diagnosis.

Assessment: osteoporosis responding to alendronate, with normal mineral and thyroid labs and adequate vitamin D.

Plan: continue alendronate and calcium/vitamin D. Repeat DXA in two years. Return to me then, sooner if she has a fracture.

Endocrinology

No chest pain, SOB, edema, dizziness.

Meds reconciled line by line with her pill organizer:
HCTZ 25 daily, amlodipine 5 daily, atorvastatin 20 qHS, methotrexate 15 mg weekly, folic acid 1 mg daily, prednisone 5 mg daily, alendronate 70 mg weekly, calcium carbonate/D3 600/400 BID, mesalamine 800 mg TID.

Labs 6/16: Ca 9.8, Cr 1.0, K 4.2. CBC normal, Hgb back to 13.2. Lipids at goal.
Most recent DXA (3/2023): lumbar spine T -2.5.

A/P:
1. Polypharmacy concern - went through what each medication is for. Each has an active indication and is managed jointly with GI, rheum and endocrine; nothing she's willing or able to drop right now. Suggested she ask GI at next visit whether mesalamine can be given in fewer daily doses.
2. HTN - continue HCTZ and amlodipine.
3. HLD, RA, UC, osteoporosis - stable, plans per specialists.
RTC 6 months.

documents.title: Oncology surveillance visit
documents.author: oncology
documents.body:
MEDICAL ONCOLOGY - SURVIVORSHIP VISIT
Patient: Arlene Jacobs   DOB 01/30/1955   Visit: 10/30/2023

History: left breast cancer treated in 2016 with lumpectomy and sentinel node biopsy; treatment complete. Seen yearly. Other history includes RA on methotrexate and prednisone, osteoporosis on alendronate, and ulcerative colitis diagnosed last December. No allergies.

She feels well. Mammogram 10/25 benign (BI-RADS 2). Exam: no breast masses, healed left breast incision, no axillary or supraclavicular adenopathy.

Surveillance labs: CA 27-29 64 U/mL (reference <38), resulted 11/1.

Plan: given the elevated tumor marker, whole-body bone scan ordered. I spoke with her by phone on 11/1 to explain why. Will see her once it is done.

Medical Oncology

reports.text: Whole-body planar imaging 3 hours after IV Tc-99m MDP. Focal increased uptake in the T7 and T10 vertebral bodies and in the right 6th and 8th ribs posterolaterally. No other abnormal skeletal uptake. Normal renal and bladder activity.
reports.conclusion: Foci of increased uptake in T7, T10 and the right 6th and 8th ribs, suspicious for osseous metastases in this patient with a history of breast cancer. Tissue sampling of an accessible lesion suggested.

reports.text: Specimen: T10 vertebral body, CT-guided core biopsy. Microscopic: bone and marrow infiltrated by nests of malignant epithelial cells. Immunohistochemical profile supports origin from the breast. Estrogen receptor positive (90% of tumor cells), progesterone receptor positive (60%), HER2 negative (IHC 1+).
reports.conclusion: Metastatic carcinoma, consistent with breast primary.

documents.title: CT-guided T10 biopsy
documents.author: interventional radiology
documents.body: CT-guided core biopsy of the T10 vertebral body, 11/20/2023. Indication: bone scan uptake suspicious for metastasis. Moderate sedation. Right posterior transpedicular approach; three 13-gauge cores obtained. No immediate complications. Patient discharged home after observation. Pathology: metastatic carcinoma consistent with breast primary; ER positive, PR positive, HER2 negative.

medications.sig: 4 mg IV over 15 minutes every 4 weeks at the oncology infusion center

documents.title: Oncology visit - metastatic recurrence
documents.author: oncology
documents.body:
MEDICAL ONCOLOGY
Patient: Arlene Jacobs   DOB 01/30/1955   Visit: 12/04/2023

Ms. Jacobs returns with results. Bone scan 11/8 showed uptake at T7, T10 and the right 6th and 8th ribs. CT-guided biopsy of T10 on 11/20: metastatic carcinoma consistent with her breast primary, ER positive (90%), PR positive (60%), HER2 negative (IHC 1+).

She has no bone pain, no neurologic symptoms. Exam: no spinal tenderness; strength and sensation normal in the legs.

Impression: recurrent hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, bone-only metastatic disease.

Plan:
1. Systemic therapy: letrozole 2.5 mg by mouth daily, starting today. Reviewed hot flashes, joint aches and bone thinning as possible effects.
2. Bone-directed therapy: stop alendronate. Start zoledronic acid 4 mg IV every 4 weeks in our infusion center, first dose today. Continue calcium/vitamin D. Renal function before each dose.
3. Restaging bone scan in about 4-5 months to judge response.
4. Dental: advised to let her dentist know she is on zoledronic acid before any dental work.
5. Long discussion with patient. She knows to call for new bone pain, weakness or numbness.

Copy to primary care, rheumatology, endocrinology.

Medical Oncology

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Primary Care Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Came in to talk through the oncology news. Breast cancer is back, in the bones of her spine and ribs, found after a high tumor marker. Started letrozole tablets daily and zoledronic acid infusions every 4 weeks last Monday. Alendronate stopped. No bone pain.

Meds updated: alendronate off; letrozole 2.5 mg daily (oncology); zoledronic acid 4 mg IV q4wk (oncology).

O: VS as charted. Composed, a little tearful. Spine nontender. Lungs clear, heart RRR. No edema.

A/P:
1. Metastatic breast cancer, bone only, hormone receptor positive - letrozole and zoledronic acid, oncology leading. Med list and problem list updated. Questions answered as best I could; deferred treatment specifics to oncology.
2. Osteoporosis - now covered by zoledronic acid; endocrine aware.
3. Coping - talked about who she can lean on; she knows she can call us any time.
4. MTX labs today; creatinine also matters for zoledronic acid.
RTC 2-3 months / AWV.
